title: Arm-separate matching cancels the aggregate trial's chance imbalance; pooled matching carries it
question: Arm-separate matching weights each individual-data arm to the corresponding aggregate arm; pooled matching uses one weight function. When does each give a biased anchored comparison, and is the bias of arm-separate matching the product of unmatched prognostic strength and aggregate arm imbalance, as the design claims?
answer: The product claim is wrong. Given an aggregate-trial imbalance kappa, pooled matching is biased by kappa (beta/2 + gamma_X + gamma_U rho_T) and arm-separate matching by kappa gamma_U (rho_T - rho_S); simulation matched both (slopes 1.00 and 0.96). Arm-separate matching reproduces the aggregate imbalance in the individual-data contrast so it cancels, and is biased only when an unmatched prognostic covariate relates to the matched one differently in the two trials. It had smaller bias than pooled matching in every scenario with an imposed imbalance and 10% to 27% lower RMSE under chance imbalance.
findings: With the matched-unmatched correlation shared between trials, arm-separate bias was within Monte Carlo error of zero in all 16 scenarios with an unmatched prognostic covariate and an imposed imbalance (largest 0.011).
Slope of simulated on predicted bias: pooled 1.004 (SE 0.011); arm-separate 0.958 (SE 0.035).
Under chance imbalance, arm-separate RMSE over pooled 0.73 to 0.90; its sandwich interval overcovered (0.965 to 0.991) because the two trials' imbalances are positively correlated.
Two-stage MAIC behaved like pooled matching, correcting the individual trial's imbalance but not the aggregate trial's.
The design's candidate diagnostic, the weighted difference in the unmatched covariate between arms, estimates rho_S kappa and cannot see rho_T; its correlation with arm-separate bias was -0.41.
not_answered: Continuous outcome, linear model, one matched and one unmatched covariate, shared effect modification; the non-collapsible case, where arm-separate matching compares arms in different populations, is not studied, and the arm-separate interval's conservatism is not repaired. Peer review has not been done.
design: Anchored MAIC with a continuous outcome, 300 per arm; 96 scenarios crossing an imposed aggregate-arm imbalance in the matched covariate (0, 0.1, 0.2 SD or chance), the unmatched covariate's prognostic strength, the matched-unmatched correlation in each trial and shared effect modification; unadjusted, pooled, arm-separate and two-stage MAIC.
estimand: Anchored B-versus-A mean difference in the target
